## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
2	\label{app:beam-search}
3	
4	OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
5	The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
6	Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.
7	
8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.

The initial 50-document DocRED subset (Table~\ref{tab:beam-search}) was subsequently validated on the full 998-document set: both models achieve DR${=}$0\% (Qwen CF${=}$4.94\%, Llama CF 8.54\%\,$\to$\,1.00\%, 88\% reduction; R-F1 $+$2.6\,pp Llama), confirming subset representativeness.

Table~\ref{tab:beam-docred-lora} reports LoRA + beam-4 results on the full DocRED dev set (998 documents), extending the fine-tuning composability evaluation from SciERC to the higher-$\bar{\kappa}$ regime.
Parse failure rates under LoRA beam-4 range from 1.3\% to 2.9\%, lower than the zero-shot rate.

\centering
\small
\caption{LoRA greedy vs.\ beam search ($k{=}4$) on DocRED (998 dev documents) under full S1 constraints.

  & Greedy con & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.26 & 84.71 & 44.70 & 2.6 \\ % d065: 4096 context
  & Beam-4 con & 0 & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{85.23} & \textbf{47.17} & \textbf{1.3} \\

\end{table}

Llama-3.1-8B achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET, RV, DR, CF = 0\%) on DocRED with LoRA + beam-4, extending the zero-violation result from SciERC to the high-$\bar{\kappa}$ regime.
Qwen3-8B achieves DR=0\% with near-zero CF (0.01\%); R-F1 is preserved ($\pm$0.06\,pp).
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

\paragraph{Latency overhead.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency} reports wall-clock latency for greedy and beam search ($k{=}4$) under LoRA fine-tuning.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{s/doc} & \textbf{Overhead} \\
\midrule
Greedy unconstrained   & 2.612 & 1.00$\times$ \\
Greedy constrained (S1)& 2.873 & 1.10$\times$ \\
Beam-4 unconstrained   & 3.446 & 1.32$\times$ \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Latency per document (SciERC, 551 docs, Qwen3-8B LoRA FT, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). Overhead relative to greedy unconstrained.}
\label{tab:beam-latency}
\end{table}

Beam search itself adds 32\% latency (4 beams); constraint overhead increases from 10\% (greedy) to 16.5\% (beam) because each beam independently maintains grammar and semantic state.
The total 1.54$\times$ overhead is acceptable for offline batch IE; \texttt{early\_stopping} limits additional compute to partial-sequence exploration.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.
5	
6	\paragraph{Grammar-constrained decoding.}
7	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and related systems~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql,park2024grammar,jsonschemabench2025} enforce format validity via CFG-based token masking.
8	In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile type systems into prefix automata, but IE type environments accumulate dynamically (\S\ref{sec:composition}).
9	
10	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
11	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie}, TANL~\cite{paolini2021tanl}, REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, and others~\cite{fei2022lasuie,wang2022deepstruct,lu2022uie,lou2023usm,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure or frame IE as structured generation, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
12	GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts, achieving structural compliance without runtime semantic enforcement; OntoCoDec complements these approaches by adding decoding-time type constraints (different paradigms; KnowCoder reports R-F1${=}$40.0 on SciERC~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} vs.\ our 45.47 with different base models).
13	
14	\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
15	\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation; EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico}, IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen}, and DCCD~\cite{dccd2026} enforce constraints via ASP, backtracking, or draft-conditioning.
16	Grammar-only enforcement (GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd}, BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}) achieves only partial DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}).
17	OntoCoDec uses forward-only token masking at $O(|V|)$ per step; extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak} despite reasoning degradation in other domains~\cite{banerjee2025crane,formattax2026}.
18

1	% Discussion paragraphs for §7

10	\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
11	Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
12	For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
13	Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
14	When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
15	% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
16	In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
17	The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.
18	
19	%%% Paragraph 2: CF Severity Argument %%%
20	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=9.90%), phase2_scierc_grammar_only (CF=0.08%),
21	%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2.57%)
22	
23	\paragraph{Severity of Cross-Field Violations.}
24	Domain/range (DR) violations produce structurally invalid triples---a triple asserting that a \emph{Task} entity fills the \emph{domain} slot of \textsc{Part-of}, which requires \emph{Method}, cannot be consumed by any downstream system without error.
25	DR violations are therefore hard constraints.
26	Cross-field consistency (CF) violations are qualitatively different: each individual triple remains type-valid with respect to its own relation's domain/range rules; only cross-triple consistency is broken when the same entity receives different types across relations.
27	The dominant conflict pattern---\emph{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\emph{OtherScientificTerm} (60 of 245~affected entities on SciERC)---reflects genuine semantic ambiguity in the type system rather than a systematic method failure.
28	% exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
29	Ablation evidence cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer: grammar-only decoding yields CF\,=\,0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline, while the full system reaches 9.90\% on SciERC and 2.57\% on DocRED
30	(Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.1-8B exhibits 12.02\% on DocRED, the highest across all configurations).
31	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_grammar_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
32	% llama_docred_full_s1: CF=0.1202
33	This arises from per-relation independent enforcement, where each relation's constraint mask is computed without access to type decisions made for other relations.
34	A natural extension is a global entity-level type consensus pass that resolves entity types before relation-specific enforcement.
35	
36	%%% Paragraph 3: F1 Significance Difference Explanation %%%
37	% exp_ids: d012_bootstrap_ci (DocRED +0.50pp p<0.001, SciERC +0.13pp p=0.58),
38	%          phase0_docred_unconstrained (RV=29.66%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (RV=1.39%)
39	
40	\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
41	The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$, 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81]) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) relation names.
42	% exp_id: d012_bootstrap_ci
43	Under the all-valid-set evaluation protocol, a predicted triple whose relation name does not appear in the ontology is counted as a false positive.
44	The DocRED baseline exhibits a relation-vocabulary (RV) violation rate of 29.66\%---5{,}189 predictions with OOV relation names---all of which become false positives under this protocol.
45	% exp_id: phase0_docred_unconstrained
46	The grammar layer eliminates these OOV predictions, removing a substantial source of false positives and yielding a statistically significant precision gain.
47	On SciERC, the baseline RV rate is only 1.39\% (24~OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
48	% exp_id: phase0_scierc_unconstrained
49	The F1 improvement on DocRED is thus a direct, mechanistically transparent consequence of vocabulary enforcement at scale, not an artifact of constraint-induced distribution shift.
50	Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\% vs.\ Qwen's 29.66\%)
51	results in fewer OOV predictions eliminated by the grammar layer,
52	yielding a smaller but directionally consistent R-F1 improvement
53	($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp), confirming that the magnitude of
54	F1 gain is proportional to the baseline OOV rate.
55	% llama_docred_unconstrained: RV=0.1603, R-F1=5.98
56	% llama_docred_full_s1: RV=0, R-F1=6.27, delta=+0.29pp
57	% qwen_docred: RV=0.2966, R-F1 delta=+0.50pp
58	
59	%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
60	% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
61	%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)
62	
63	\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
64	Post-hoc filtering---generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions---yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
65	% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
66	However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
67	On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions), reducing recall from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
68	% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
69	Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
70	% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
71	OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
72	The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

\label{sec:downstream-impact}
Among constraint-removed triples, only 0.49\% match gold labels on average (``lucky violations''), confirming $<$0.5\% recall cost; on Llama SciERC all five are recovered via legal type paths (zero churn; Appendix~\ref{app:lucky-violations}).

4	\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}
5	
6	%%% CF Dual Mechanism %%%
7	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
8	
9	\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
10	CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
11	(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
12	The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
13	(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.
14	
15	These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
16	Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
17	Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
18	This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
19	The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.
20	
21	%%% Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage %%%
22	% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (final data)
23	
24	\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
25	\label{app:fallback-coverage}
26	The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
27	\emph{Grammar-first fallback} occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations.
28	The token-level fallback rate (36.6\% on SciERC Llama) is inflated by continuation tokens of multi-token type names (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 BPE tokens); at semantically meaningful first-token positions, the rate is 0.04--5.7\% (zero-shot) and drops to $\leq$\,0.11\% under fine-tuning.
29	These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
30	\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
31	Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.
32	
33	We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
34	On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
35	On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
36	The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
37	DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
38	This metric directly quantifies the empirical enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
39	Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).
40	
41	%%% Fallback Causal Tracing %%%
42	% exp_ids: Task C causal tracing (Qwen/Llama × ZS/FT × S1)
43	
44	\paragraph{Fallback Causal Tracing.}
45	\label{app:causal-tracing}
46	
47	To establish that grammar-first fallback is the \emph{sole} mechanism producing residual DR violations, we instrument the constraint processor to log, for each violation, whether the semantic mask was active ($S(t) \cap G(t) \neq \emptyset$) or bypassed via fallback ($S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$) at the type-bearing position.
48	Table~\ref{tab:causal-tracing} reports the results across four SciERC configurations.
49	
50	\begin{table}[t]
51	\centering
52	\small
53	\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrr@{}}
54	\toprule
55	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Fallback Rate} & \textbf{DR} & \textbf{From FB} \\
56	\midrule
57	Qwen3-8B  & FT S1 & 0/2256 (0\%)    & 0  & N/A \\
58	Qwen3-8B  & ZS S1 & 16/3458 (0.46\%) & 16 & 100\% \\
59	Llama-3.1-8B & FT S1 & 1/2162 (0.05\%) & 1  & 100\% \\
60	Llama-3.1-8B & ZS S1 & 1/2630 (0.04\%) & 1  & 100\% \\
61	\bottomrule
62	\end{tabular}
63	\caption{Fallback causal tracing on SciERC (551 documents). Fallback Rate: type-bearing positions where $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ triggers grammar-first fallback. DR: residual domain/range violations. From FB: fraction of DR violations occurring at fallback positions. All violations occur exclusively at tail\_type positions (range constraints are tighter than domain constraints).}
64	\label{tab:causal-tracing}
65	\end{table}
66	
67	When the semantic mask is active, $\text{DR}_{\text{independent}} = 0$: the type constraint processor structurally prevents domain/range violations.
68	All 18 residual DR violations across four configurations occur exclusively at fallback positions, confirming that grammar-first fallback is a necessary condition for residual DR.
69	Fine-tuning reduces fallback to near-zero ($\leq$0.05\%), effectively eliminating the sole source of residual violations.
70	All fallback events occur at tail\_type positions, where $|\operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)|$ is smaller than $|\operatorname{dom}(r)|$, making the intersection $S(t) \cap G(t)$ more likely to be empty.
71	
72	%%% CF-DR Trade-off Analysis %%%
73	% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (CF fallback vs full_s1 baseline)
74	
75	\paragraph{CF-DR Trade-off Analysis.}
76	\label{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}
77	
78	CF violations are the most prominent residual limitation of OntoCoDec under zero-shot decoding (9.90\% on SciERC, up to 12.02\% on Llama DocRED).
79	We treat this honestly: per-relation independent enforcement cannot eliminate CF without trading it against DR.
80	Table~\ref{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff} reports a pilot ablation in which we replace the grammar-first fallback with a CF-priority fallback that forces the entity's registered type when it conflicts with $\sigma(r)$.
81	
82	\begin{table}[t]
83	\centering
84	\small
85	\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrr@{}}
86	\toprule
87	\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{DR\,(\%)} & \textbf{CF\,(\%)} & \textbf{DR+CF} & \textbf{$f_{\text{gf}}$\,(\%)} \\
88	\midrule
89	Full S1 (baseline) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 10.83 & --- \\
90	CF fallback        & 14.78 & 0.04 & 14.82 & 36.64 \\
91	\midrule
92	$\Delta$ & $+$13.85 & $-$9.86 & $+$3.99 & --- \\
93	\bottomrule
94	\end{tabular}
95	\caption{CF-DR trade-off pilot on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, 551 documents; \texttt{w1\_cf\_fallback\_scierc\_pilot}). CF fallback eliminates CF but re-routes violations to DR, increasing total violations (DR+CF) by 3.99\,pp. $f_{\text{gf}}$: token-level grammar-first fallback rate at type-bearing positions (includes continuation tokens of multi-token type names; first-token position fallback rate is 0.46\% for SciERC Qwen; \S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}).}
96	\label{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff}
97	\end{table}
98	
99	The CF fallback variant nearly eliminates CF (9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.04\%, $-$9.86\,pp) but at the cost of a 15.9$\times$ increase in DR (0.93\%\,$\to$\,14.78\%, $+$13.85\,pp).
100	% exp_id: w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004, f_gf=0.3664
101	This is not a net improvement: total violations (DR+CF) rise from 10.83\% to 14.82\% ($+$3.99\,pp), so the change \emph{re-routes} violations rather than reducing them.
102	The mechanism is mechanical: each token position with conflicting masks must commit to one violation type; when the CF fallback forces the system to emit the entity's registered type even though it lies outside $\sigma(r)$, the resulting triple satisfies cross-entity consistency but violates domain/range.
103	The token-level grammar-first fallback is triggered at 36.64\% of type-bearing positions (0.46\% at first-token positions; \S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}); this conflict is structural, not a tunable hyperparameter.
104	
105	We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
106	Within this design, the current full S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.
107	The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are descriptively inversely associated, with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}); however, $n{=}6$ is insufficient for statistical inference on this correlation.
108	The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.
109	While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.
110	The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.
111	
112	Two complementary paths can lower CF without re-routing it to DR.
113	(i)~\emph{Reduce the baseline conflict rate.} Composing OntoCoDec with LoRA fine-tuning on SciERC reduces CF by 88\% relative to the zero-shot setting (9.90\%\,$\to$\,1.18\%; Table~\ref{tab:composability}), because the fine-tuned model's per-slot type predictions agree more often with the entity registry, so the per-relation mask and the registry intersect more frequently.
114	% exp_id: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: CF=0.0118
115	The remaining 1.18\% still traces to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity, so this path is empirically validated on one dataset and one fine-tuning method but does not generalize without further evidence.
116	(ii)~\emph{Replace per-relation enforcement with global entity-level type consensus during decoding.} This is outside the scope of OntoCoDec's forward-only autoregressive design and is left to future work.
117	
118	%%% Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis %%%
119	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1,
120	%          llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
121	
122	\paragraph{Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis.}
123	\label{app:dual-factor}
124	
125	Figure~\ref{fig:dual-factor-scatter} plots residual DR against the product $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ for model$\times$dataset configurations.
126	For \emph{calibrated} models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B; unconstrained ET${<}$3\% on both datasets), a linear fit yields $y = 0.366x - 0.138$ with $R^2 = 0.886$ ($n{=}4$, $F(1,2) = 15.54$, $p \approx 0.058$); with only four data points (df $= 2$) and $p > 0.05$, this constitutes a descriptive characterization rather than a confirmatory statistical test.
127	The strong fit supports the dual-factor pattern from \S\ref{sec:composition}: residual DR is governed by the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate.
128	Mistral-7B (unconstrained ET${=}$7.58\% on DocRED) deviates from this pattern: its residual DR on DocRED (33.21\%) substantially exceeds the linear prediction. When model calibration is insufficient (ET${>}$5\% on either dataset), residual DR is dominated by entity misclassification rather than constraint-search failure.
129	This motivates a principled exclusion criterion: models with unconstrained ET${>}$5\% on either dataset fall outside the regime where the tightness$\times$RV product is the primary DR driver.
130	The two DocRED points (high $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) separate cleanly from the two SciERC points (low $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), and within each dataset the model with higher baseline RV shows higher residual DR.
131	
132	\begin{figure}[t]
133	\centering
134	\includegraphics[width=0.75\columnwidth]{figures/dual_factor_scatter.pdf}
135	\caption{Residual DR vs.\ Schema Restrictiveness $\times$ Baseline Violation Rate ($\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$) across four model$\times$dataset configurations.
136	Linear fit (calibrated models): $y = 0.366x - 0.138$, $R^2 = 0.886$; Mistral deviates due to entity misclassification.}
137	\label{fig:dual-factor-scatter}
138	\end{figure}
139	
140	%%% Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact (moved from §7) %%%
141	% exp_ids: d012_bootstrap_ci (DocRED +0.50pp p<0.001, SciERC +0.13pp p=0.58),
142	%          phase0_docred_unconstrained (RV=29.66%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (RV=1.39%)
143	
144	\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
145	The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary relation names.
146	DocRED's baseline RV of 29.66\% produces 5{,}189 OOV predictions counted as false positives; eliminating them yields a significant precision gain.
147	SciERC's baseline RV is only 1.39\% (24 OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
148	Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\%) yields a smaller but directionally consistent improvement ($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp); F1 gain magnitude is proportional to baseline OOV rate.
149	% exp_ids: phase0_docred_unconstrained, phase0_scierc_unconstrained
150	% exp_ids: llama_docred_unconstrained (RV=16.03%), llama_docred_full_s1 (R-F1 delta=+0.29pp)
151	
152	%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
153	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%),
154	%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained (DR=15.37%), phase2_docred_unconstrained (DR=18.46%)
155	
156	\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
157	Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
158	For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
159	Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
160	Even after LoRA fine-tuning, residual DR of 1--2\% persists on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); constraints remain necessary at deployment-grade quality.
161	% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval
162	In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
163	The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting stress-tests constraint robustness under maximum model uncertainty, while composability with fine-tuning (\S\ref{sec:composability}) validates practical deployment value.
164	
165	%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
166	% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
167	%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)
168	
169	\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
170	Post-hoc filtering (generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions) yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
171	% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
172	However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
173	On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions); recall drops from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
174	% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
175	Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
176	% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
177	OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
178	The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.
179

181	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=245), llama_scierc_full_s1 (CF=162),

184	\paragraph{Cross-Field Violation Distribution.}
185	\label{app:cf-distribution}
186	
187	Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution} reports the complete distribution of conflicting-type pairs for SciERC full S1 (245 CF violations, all pairwise; no mention triggered $\geq$3 types).
188	Conflicts involving the \textsc{Generic} type account for 63.3\% (155/245) of all violations.
189	\textsc{Generic} is SciERC's anaphoric/placeholder label (``this approach'', ``the method''), which competes with every content type depending on whether the mention is used anaphorically or referentially, a distinction the per-slot constrained decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.
190	
191	The pattern generalizes across models and datasets: on Llama-3.1-8B SciERC, \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\textsc{OtherScientificTerm} remains the top pair (53/162, 32.7\%); on DocRED, the analogous catch-all type \textsc{MISC} drives 76.6\% of Qwen's CF violations.
192	Under unconstrained decoding, CF rates collapse to $\leq$1\% on both datasets; CF violations are a side-effect of per-slot type commitment rather than a model deficiency.

314	\paragraph{Residual DR Error Analysis.}
315	\label{app:residual-dr-analysis}
316	
317	Across all fine-tuned settings (2 models $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ full S1), only 36 domain/range violations remain.
318	Manual inspection reveals four root causes:
319	
320	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
321	\item \emph{Entity type errors} (39\%): the LLM assigns an incorrect entity type (e.g., labeling a geographic entity as \textsc{LOC} when the gold standard requires \textsc{MISC}), causing the semantic mask to permit a domain/range-incompatible relation.
322	\item \emph{Schema coverage gaps} (33\%): the frequency-based constraint table, constructed from training-set co-occurrence statistics, does not cover long-tail type pairs that are ontologically valid but rare. These violations are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone.
323	\item \emph{Incorrect relation selection} (17\%): the model selects a semantically inappropriate relation whose domain/range constraints are incompatible with the correctly typed entities.
324	\item \emph{Direction reversal} (11\%): the model assigns the correct relation but inverts head/tail roles, placing entities in positions that violate the relation's asymmetric domain/range specification.
325	\end{enumerate}
326	
327	Two dataset-specific patterns emerge.
328	Outside Llama DocRED, all residual violations (3 of 36, spanning Llama SciERC and Qwen DocRED) trace exclusively to schema coverage gaps: the model's entity typing is accurate, and the constraint system has reached its theoretical ceiling given the frequency-based constraint table.
329	On DocRED, Llama-3.1-8B contributes 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), with entity type errors as the dominant cause (14/33, 42\%).
330	This asymmetry reflects Llama's weaker fine-tuned entity typing on DocRED's larger ontology (96 relations, 7 entity types) compared to Qwen, which achieves near-zero residual.
331	The implication is twofold: (i)~the irreducible floor from schema gaps is small ($\sim$3 violations across 4 settings), so the constraint system operates near its theoretical optimum; (ii)~residual violations from entity typing errors are addressable through stronger base models or improved entity typing modules, without modifying the constraint architecture.

% Appendix B — Extended Discussion

\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}

%%% CF Dual Mechanism %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1

\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.

These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.

%%% Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage %%%
% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (final data)

\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
\label{app:fallback-coverage}
The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
\emph{Grammar-first fallback} occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations.
The token-level fallback rate (36.6\% on SciERC Llama) is inflated by continuation tokens of multi-token type names (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 BPE tokens); at semantically meaningful first-token positions, the rate is 0.04--5.7\% (zero-shot) and drops to $\leq$\,0.11\% under fine-tuning.
These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.

We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
This metric directly quantifies the empirical enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).

%%% Fallback Causal Tracing %%%
% exp_ids: Task C causal tracing (Qwen/Llama × ZS/FT × S1)

\paragraph{Fallback Causal Tracing.}
\label{app:causal-tracing}

To establish that grammar-first fallback is the \emph{sole} mechanism producing residual DR violations, we instrument the constraint processor to log, for each violation, whether the semantic mask was active ($S(t) \cap G(t) \neq \emptyset$) or bypassed via fallback ($S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$) at the type-bearing position.
Table~\ref{tab:causal-tracing} reports the results across four SciERC configurations.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Fallback Rate} & \textbf{DR} & \textbf{From FB} \\
\midrule
Qwen3-8B  & FT S1 & 0/2256 (0\%)    & 0  & N/A \\
Qwen3-8B  & ZS S1 & 16/3458 (0.46\%) & 16 & 100\% \\
Llama-3.1-8B & FT S1 & 1/2162 (0.05\%) & 1  & 100\% \\
Llama-3.1-8B & ZS S1 & 1/2630 (0.04\%) & 1  & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Fallback causal tracing on SciERC (551 documents). Fallback Rate: type-bearing positions where $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ triggers grammar-first fallback. DR: residual domain/range violations. From FB: fraction of DR violations occurring at fallback positions. All violations occur exclusively at tail\_type positions (range constraints are tighter than domain constraints).}
\label{tab:causal-tracing}
\end{table}

When the semantic mask is active, $\text{DR}_{\text{independent}} = 0$: the type constraint processor structurally prevents domain/range violations.
All 18 residual DR violations across four configurations occur exclusively at fallback positions, confirming that grammar-first fallback is a necessary condition for residual DR.
Fine-tuning reduces fallback to near-zero ($\leq$0.05\%), effectively eliminating the sole source of residual violations.
All fallback events occur at tail\_type positions, where $|\operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)|$ is smaller than $|\operatorname{dom}(r)|$, making the intersection $S(t) \cap G(t)$ more likely to be empty.

%%% CF-DR Trade-off Analysis %%%
% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (CF fallback vs full_s1 baseline)

\paragraph{CF-DR Trade-off Analysis.}
\label{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}

CF violations are the most prominent residual limitation of OntoCoDec under zero-shot decoding (9.90\% on SciERC, up to 12.02\% on Llama DocRED).
We treat this honestly: per-relation independent enforcement cannot eliminate CF without trading it against DR.
Table~\ref{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff} reports a pilot ablation in which we replace the grammar-first fallback with a CF-priority fallback that forces the entity's registered type when it conflicts with $\sigma(r)$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{DR\,(\%)} & \textbf{CF\,(\%)} & \textbf{DR+CF} & \textbf{$f_{\text{gf}}$\,(\%)} \\
\midrule
Full S1 (baseline) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 10.83 & --- \\
CF fallback        & 14.78 & 0.04 & 14.82 & 36.64 \\
\midrule
$\Delta$ & $+$13.85 & $-$9.86 & $+$3.99 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{CF-DR trade-off pilot on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, 551 documents; \texttt{w1\_cf\_fallback\_scierc\_pilot}). CF fallback eliminates CF but re-routes violations to DR, increasing total violations (DR+CF) by 3.99\,pp. $f_{\text{gf}}$: token-level grammar-first fallback rate at type-bearing positions (includes continuation tokens of multi-token type names; first-token position fallback rate is 0.46\% for SciERC Qwen; \S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}).}
\label{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff}
\end{table}

The CF fallback variant nearly eliminates CF (9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.04\%, $-$9.86\,pp) but at the cost of a 15.9$\times$ increase in DR (0.93\%\,$\to$\,14.78\%, $+$13.85\,pp).
% exp_id: w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004, f_gf=0.3664
This is not a net improvement: total violations (DR+CF) rise from 10.83\% to 14.82\% ($+$3.99\,pp), so the change \emph{re-routes} violations rather than reducing them.
The mechanism is mechanical: each token position with conflicting masks must commit to one violation type; when the CF fallback forces the system to emit the entity's registered type even though it lies outside $\sigma(r)$, the resulting triple satisfies cross-entity consistency but violates domain/range.
The token-level grammar-first fallback is triggered at 36.64\% of type-bearing positions (0.46\% at first-token positions; \S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}); this conflict is structural, not a tunable hyperparameter.

We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
Within this design, the current full S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.
The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are descriptively inversely associated, with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}); however, $n{=}6$ is insufficient for statistical inference on this correlation.
The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.
While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.
The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.

Two complementary paths can lower CF without re-routing it to DR.
(i)~\emph{Reduce the baseline conflict rate.} Composing OntoCoDec with LoRA fine-tuning on SciERC reduces CF by 88\% relative to the zero-shot setting (9.90\%\,$\to$\,1.18\%; Table~\ref{tab:composability}), because the fine-tuned model's per-slot type predictions agree more often with the entity registry, so the per-relation mask and the registry intersect more frequently.
% exp_id: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: CF=0.0118
The remaining 1.18\% still traces to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity, so this path is empirically validated on one dataset and one fine-tuning method but does not generalize without further evidence.
(ii)~\emph{Replace per-relation enforcement with global entity-level type consensus during decoding.} This is outside the scope of OntoCoDec's forward-only autoregressive design and is left to future work.

\paragraph{Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis.}
\label{app:dual-factor}

Figure~\ref{fig:dual-factor-scatter} plots residual DR against the product $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ for model$\times$dataset configurations.
For \emph{calibrated} models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B; unconstrained ET${<}$3\% on both datasets), a linear fit yields $y = 0.366x - 0.138$ with $R^2 = 0.886$ ($n{=}4$, $F(1,2) = 15.54$, $p \approx 0.058$); with only four data points (df $= 2$) and $p > 0.05$, this constitutes a descriptive characterization rather than a confirmatory statistical test.
The strong fit supports the dual-factor pattern from \S\ref{sec:composition}: residual DR is governed by the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate.
Mistral-7B (unconstrained ET${=}$7.58\% on DocRED) deviates from this pattern: its residual DR on DocRED (33.21\%) substantially exceeds the linear prediction. When model calibration is insufficient (ET${>}$5\% on either dataset), residual DR is dominated by entity misclassification rather than constraint-search failure.
This motivates a principled exclusion criterion: models with unconstrained ET${>}$5\% on either dataset fall outside the regime where the tightness$\times$RV product is the primary DR driver.
The two DocRED points (high $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) separate cleanly from the two SciERC points (low $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), and within each dataset the model with higher baseline RV shows higher residual DR.

\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary relation names.
DocRED's baseline RV of 29.66\% produces 5{,}189 OOV predictions counted as false positives; eliminating them yields a significant precision gain.
SciERC's baseline RV is only 1.39\% (24 OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\%) yields a smaller but directionally consistent improvement ($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp); F1 gain magnitude is proportional to baseline OOV rate.

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
Even after LoRA fine-tuning, residual DR of 1--2\% persists on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); constraints remain necessary at deployment-grade quality.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting stress-tests constraint robustness under maximum model uncertainty, while composability with fine-tuning (\S\ref{sec:composability}) validates practical deployment value.

%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%

%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)

\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
Post-hoc filtering (generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions) yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions); recall drops from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

\paragraph{Residual DR Error Analysis.}
\label{app:residual-dr-analysis}

Across all fine-tuned settings (2 models $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ full S1), only 36 domain/range violations remain.
Manual inspection reveals four root causes:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Entity type errors} (39\%): the LLM assigns an incorrect entity type (e.g., labeling a geographic entity as \textsc{LOC} when the gold standard requires \textsc{MISC}), causing the semantic mask to permit a domain/range-incompatible relation.
\item \emph{Schema coverage gaps} (33\%): the frequency-based constraint table, constructed from training-set co-occurrence statistics, does not cover long-tail type pairs that are ontologically valid but rare. These violations are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone.
\item \emph{Incorrect relation selection} (17\%): the model selects a semantically inappropriate relation whose domain/range constraints are incompatible with the correctly typed entities.
\item \emph{Direction reversal} (11\%): the model assigns the correct relation but inverts head/tail roles, placing entities in positions that violate the relation's asymmetric domain/range specification.
\end{enumerate}

Two dataset-specific patterns emerge.
Outside Llama DocRED, all residual violations (3 of 36, spanning Llama SciERC and Qwen DocRED) trace exclusively to schema coverage gaps: the model's entity typing is accurate, and the constraint system has reached its theoretical ceiling given the frequency-based constraint table.
On DocRED, Llama-3.1-8B contributes 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), with entity type errors as the dominant cause (14/33, 42\%).
This asymmetry reflects Llama's weaker fine-tuned entity typing on DocRED's larger ontology (96 relations, 7 entity types) compared to Qwen, which achieves near-zero residual.
The implication is twofold: (i)~the irreducible floor from schema gaps is small ($\sim$3 violations across 4 settings), so the constraint system operates near its theoretical optimum; (ii)~residual violations from entity typing errors are addressable through stronger base models or improved entity typing modules, without modifying the constraint architecture.

%%% Fuzzy Relation Matching %%%

\paragraph{Relation Matching Protocol.}
\label{app:fuzzy-matching}
Relation F1 evaluation uses fuzzy normalization to handle model-specific formatting variants (e.g., underscores vs.\ spaces, abbreviations).
A predicted relation $r_p$ matches gold relation $r_g$ if: (1)~exact string match after case-insensitive normalization, or (2)~token overlap $>$80\% \emph{and} edit distance $\leq 2$.
This protocol affects primarily Mistral, which produces underscore-separated variants (e.g., ``head\_of\_government'' for ``head of government'').
On Mistral DocRED, fuzzy matching contributes 98 additional TPs ($+$0.84\,pp R-F1; strict R-F1\,=\,3.50\% vs.\ fuzzy 4.34\%).
For Qwen and Llama under grammar constraints, the grammar layer enforces exact relation names, making fuzzy matching irrelevant (0 additional matches).
All F1 figures in the main text use fuzzy normalization consistently across all models and conditions.

\paragraph{WikiEvents Dataset Details.}
\label{app:wikievents}
WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} is a document-level event argument extraction benchmark grounded in the DARPA KAIROS ontology.
It defines 56 event types, 80 argument roles, and 27 entity types, with 245 (event\_type, role)$\to$allowed\_entity\_types constraints.
The grammar layer targets EV (event vocabulary), RoV (role vocabulary), and ET; the semantic layer enforces AC (argument constraint) via role-conditioned masking, analogous to RE domain/range enforcement.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness in WikiEvents.}
\label{app:wikievents-kappa}
% Data source: artifacts/w1c_wikievents_kappa_results.md
WikiEvents role-level tightness (with $|\mathcal{E}|{=}27$) has mean $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$ and median 0.89; 84\% of roles have $\kappa \geq 0.80$ (4 or fewer valid entity types out of 27).
The tightness-violation pattern extends to event extraction: roles with $\kappa \geq 0.90$ exhibit the highest AC rate (50\%), compared to 21\% for medium-tightness ($0.80 \leq \kappa < 0.90$) and 30\% for loose ($\kappa < 0.80$) roles; this is consistent with the RE observation that constraint tightness correlates with violation frequency.
However, the correlation is modulated by entity type prototypicality: semantically intuitive roles (e.g., Transportation.Vehicle$\to$VEH) show 0\% AC despite $\kappa{=}0.963$, while roles that require rare KAIROS-specific types (e.g., Crime$\to$CRM, Sentence$\to$SEN) show near-100\% AC because LLMs default to common types (PER, ORG).
The loose group's elevated rate (30\%) is driven by high-frequency roles such as Attack.Target (126 args, 34\% AC, $\kappa{=}0.59$), where systematic model errors outweigh the permissive constraint space.

\paragraph{Lucky Violation Analysis.}
\label{app:lucky-violations}
Table~\ref{tab:lucky-violations} quantifies the recall cost of DR elimination.
A ``lucky violation'' is a constraint-removed triple that happens to match a gold label---an ontologically invalid prediction that is nonetheless correct.
Across four fine-tuned configurations, lucky violations average 0.49\% of gold triples (range 0.01--0.51\%), confirming that nearly all removed DR violations are false positives.
On Llama SciERC, all five lucky violations are recovered as legal type paths under constrained decoding (zero churn): the model finds an ontology-compliant route to the same prediction.

\paragraph{Trie-Only Baseline (GCD-Equivalent).}
\label{app:trie-baseline}
Table~\ref{tab:trie-baseline} isolates the effect of vocabulary membership constraints without JSON structural enforcement.
The trie constrains entity type and relation tokens to schema-valid values (achieving ET${=}$0\%, RV${=}$0\% across all configurations), functionally equivalent to GCD's~\cite{geng2023gcd} constrained decoding.
However, without grammar-level JSON enforcement, models systematically omit entity type fields (83\% of triples) or produce malformed JSON (0--51\% parse failure), causing DR to rise to 15--96\%---far worse than unconstrained baselines.
This confirms the grammar layer is a structural prerequisite: vocabulary constraints operate correctly in isolation but require JSON scaffolding to reach the positions where they apply.

% Appendix: Post-hoc Type Consistency Resolution (TCR)
% exp_ids: d065_tcr_pilot (all 10 configs)

\section{Post-hoc Type Consistency Resolution}
\label{app:tcr}

S1 enforces domain/range constraints per-triple but does not enforce global entity type consensus, leaving residual CF violations where the same entity receives different types across triples.
We evaluate a post-hoc resolution step (TCR): for each entity with conflicting type assignments, TCR selects the type that maximizes satisfaction count across all relations referencing that entity, subject to domain/range constraints.
Unlike naive majority voting (which ignores relational constraints and increases DR), TCR is constraint-aware: candidate types are scored by how many of the entity's relational contexts they satisfy.
TCR runs after S1 decoding completes and has access to the full document context.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: TCR results on SciERC
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rr rr r r@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CF (\%)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{DR (\%)}} & \textbf{$\Delta$E-F1} & \textbf{Fund.} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-7} \cmidrule(l){8-8}
\textbf{Config} & \textbf{Model} & Pre & Post & Pre & Post & (pp) & (\%) \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Zero-shot}
  & Qwen    & 9.75 & \textbf{0} & 0.93  & 1.21  & $-$1.29 & 2.04 \\
  & Llama   & 6.40 & \textbf{0} & 0.08  & 0.30  & $-$1.78 & 1.85 \\
  & Mistral & 0.67 & \textbf{0} & 13.36 & 12.87 & $+$0.05 & 0 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{LoRA}
  & Qwen    & 1.19 & \textbf{0} & 0     & 0     & $-$0.75 & 0 \\
  & Llama   & 0.46 & \textbf{0} & 0.09  & 0.09  & $-$0.18 & 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{TCR on SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 551 docs).
Pre/Post: before/after TCR.
$\Delta$E-F1: entity F1 change (F1$\times$100).
Fund.: percentage of conflicting entities where no single type satisfies all relational constraints (fundamental conflicts).
TCR eliminates all CF with DR increases $\leq$0.28\,pp; fundamental conflicts are 0--2\%.}
\label{tab:tcr-scierc}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: TCR results on DocRED
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll rr rr r r@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CF (\%)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{DR (\%)}} & \textbf{$\Delta$E-F1} & \textbf{Fund.} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-7} \cmidrule(l){8-8}
\textbf{Config} & \textbf{Model} & Pre & Post & Pre & Post & (pp) & (\%) \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Zero-shot}
  & Qwen    & 13.11 & \textbf{0} & 10.21 & 11.74 & $-$3.44 & 13.52 \\
  & Llama   & 23.71 & \textbf{0} &  2.55 & 11.93 & $-$5.21 & 22.78 \\
  & 70B     & 11.61 & \textbf{0} &  0    &  4.20 & $-$5.98 & 18.26 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{LoRA}
  & Qwen    &  0.42 & \textbf{0} &  0.01 &  0.14 & $-$0.16 & 12.16 \\
  & Llama   &  0.36 & \textbf{0} &  0.21 &  0.20 & $-$0.17 & 11.59 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{TCR on DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 998 docs).
Under zero-shot, TCR introduces substantial DR regressions (up to $+$9.38\,pp for Llama) and E-F1 drops (up to $-$5.98\,pp for 70B).
Fundamental conflict rates are 12--23\%, an order of magnitude higher than SciERC.
Under LoRA, low baseline CF (0.36--0.42\%) limits both TCR impact and DR cost.}
\label{tab:tcr-docred}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Analysis.}
TCR effectiveness correlates inversely with schema constraint tightness $\bar{\kappa}$.
On SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), fundamental conflicts constitute 0--2\% of type disagreements: most conflicts are resolvable because the loose schema admits many valid type pairs, and TCR can find a type satisfying all relational contexts.
DR increases are bounded ($\leq$0.28\,pp), and E-F1 cost is modest ($\leq$1.78\,pp in zero-shot, $\leq$0.75\,pp under LoRA).
On DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), 13--23\% of conflicts are fundamental: the tight schema renders most type pairs invalid, so unifying an entity's type across all its relational contexts inevitably violates some domain/range constraints.
This produces severe DR regressions under zero-shot (Llama: 2.55\%$\to$11.93\%; 70B: 0\%$\to$4.20\%), where baseline CF is high enough that many entities require resolution.
Under LoRA, baseline CF is already low (0.36--0.42\%), limiting both the scope for TCR improvement and the DR cost.

This $\bar{\kappa}$-dependent boundary is consistent with the constraint tightness analysis in \S\ref{sec:composition}: $\bar{\kappa}$ characterizes not only the decoding-time DR residual regime but also the feasibility of post-hoc type resolution.
Beam search (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}) resolves CF and DR simultaneously across all $\bar{\kappa}$ values (SciERC and DocRED (998 docs): DR$\to$0\% for calibrated models), making it the preferred approach for high-tightness schemas.
TCR is a zero-cost complement for low-tightness schemas where beam search latency (1.54$\times$) is undesirable.

input.old_string: GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts, achieving structural compliance without runtime semantic enforcement; OntoCoDec complements these approaches by adding decoding-time type constraints (different paradigms; KnowCoder reports R-F1${=}$40.0 on SciERC~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} vs.\ our 45.47 with different base models).
input.new_string:
GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts, achieving structural compliance without runtime semantic enforcement.
On SciERC, GoLLIE-7B achieves zero DR violations via its Python dataclass output format but at severe coverage cost: E-F1${=}$9.17, R-F1${=}$0.0, with 46\% of documents producing empty output; OntoCoDec with LoRA (Llama-3.1-8B) achieves R-F1${=}$45.47 with DR${=}$0.09\%, surpassing KnowCoder-7B's supervised R-F1${=}$40.0~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}.
The two paradigms are complementary: GoLLIE constrains output format (structural compliance), while OntoCoDec constrains content generation (semantic compliance).

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) compiles ontology constraints into grammars ensuring JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) interprets type constraints at runtime via stateful token masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning, with rates characterized by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\kappa}$), a descriptive metric correlating schema restrictiveness with enforcement outcomes ($n{=}3$ schemas).
The two layers exhibit an empirical enabling dependency (Proposition~1): neither achieves this reduction alone.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with LoRA fine-tuning on well-calibrated models, \textsc{OntoCoDec} near-eliminates DR (92--100\% reduction, $<$0.5\% true-positive loss) with negligible RE R-F1 impact ($\pm$0.6\,pp) but introduces CF violations as a trade-off ($\leq$1.3\% fine-tuned); zero-shot effectiveness varies by dataset and model calibration (45--99\% DR reduction, 0--21.1\% CF; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).
Beam search eliminates residual DR; CF effects are configuration-dependent, with full elimination on SciERC under LoRA (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
The framework is validated on RE (SciERC, DocRED) with preliminary event extraction results on WikiEvents, across four autoregressive LMs (7--70B; 70B as feasibility check in INT4 only, \S\ref{sec:70b-results}) with logits access and three tokenizer families (up to 96 relation types).
\end{abstract}

Composed with LoRA fine-tuning on well-calibrated models, \textsc{OntoCoDec} near-eliminates DR (92--100\% reduction, $<$0.5\% true-positive loss) with negligible RE R-F1 impact ($\pm$0.6\,pp) but introduces CF violations as a trade-off ($\leq$1.3\% fine-tuned); zero-shot effectiveness varies by dataset and model calibration (45--99\% DR reduction, 0--21.1\% CF; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).
Beam search eliminates residual DR; CF effects are configuration-dependent, with full elimination on SciERC under LoRA (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
The framework is validated on RE (SciERC, DocRED) with preliminary event extraction results on WikiEvents, across four autoregressive LMs (7--70B; 70B as feasibility check in INT4 only, \S\ref{sec:70b-results}) with logits access and three tokenizer families (up to 96 relation types).
